raw_plan.interpretation: Read literally: one (1) acquisition email, in English, to the selected audience — a course creator or coach collecting student proof — asking for the documented self-serve next action (start free at app.senja.io/signup). Relationship is unknown, so it is written as a first conversation with someone who already knows testimonials matter (solution_aware) and does not yet use Senja. The dossier narrows the usable slice to cohort-based course operators, so the reader is a creator who sells a course or cohort and publishes student proof on that page; I have kept the audience name the user selected and scoped the argument to that slice. I have not assumed an imminent launch date, a failed previous ask, a particular course platform, or any installed tool. The strategy comes from the prior campaign's rework note and the verified problems: the ask that never goes out is the second one, and the second ask is a setting (at most three reminders, 1, 3 and 7 days, only to students who have not answered), not a question of nerve.

intent.reason_now: The reader is a course or cohort operator who needs student proof for the page that sells the next run. Nothing in the material establishes a deadline for this recipient, so the email earns the click on the mechanics of asking, not on urgency.
intent.desired_action: Start a free Senja account, build the student testimonial form, and turn on bounded follow-ups before sending the invites.

raw_plan.reader: A course creator or coach who sells a course or cohort and wants student text and video proof on the page that sells the next run. They are solution_aware: they already believe testimonials help and are unsure how to ask — whether to push for video, whether to ask twice, and how to do it without feeling pushy. Nothing is known about their course platform, their list size, their launch date, or any tool they currently use, so none of that may be asserted.

raw_plan.reader_scope: Cohort-based course operators (the dossier's qualified slice): creators who run a course or cohort and publish student testimonials on the page that sells it. Do not generalise the argument's fit to every member of the broader creator/coach segment.
raw_plan.promise: The second ask — the one that actually produces the testimonial — stops being something you have to work up the nerve for each time, and becomes a bounded setting you configure once before the invites go out.
raw_plan.orientation: Senja is a tool for asking your students for a text or video testimonial and reusing what comes back on the page that sells your next cohort.
raw_plan.arc: Single email. It opens on the ask that does not get sent — the follow-up — names it as a setting rather than a nerve problem, shows the exact bounds (up to three emails at 1, 3 and 7 days, only to students who have not answered, pausable for one named student), and asks for a free account so the reader can set that up before their next round of invites.
raw_plan.sequence_rationale: One email was requested in so many words, so everything load-bearing has to be in it: the reader's actual hesitation (asking again feels pushy), the mechanic that answers it (bounded, non-responder-only follow-ups), and the control that answers the fear of over-chasing (pause for one person). I led with the follow-up rather than with collection breadth because the verified problems are about asking — P1 (does not know how to get testimonials, does not want to seem pushy) and P3 (praise does not become testimony unless you ask, and ask promptly) — and because the ledger carries an exact, checkable schedule for it. Both P1 and P3 are PARTIAL fits, so the email argues that Senja gives you a way to ask again on a fixed schedule, and never that students will respond, feel fine about it, or produce stronger testimony as a result. The one assigned objection is about control over automated mail to people the reader knows personally, which the evidence can answer precisely; the objection the evidence cannot answer (how students perceive being reminded) is pushed into must_not_say rather than handed to the writer. The alternative proposition bets on the other verified problem instead — P2's format and consent uncertainty — so if the follow-up angle does not land, the untried argument is a different reason to act, not a rewording.

emails.selection_reason: The reader's documented problem is the asking, not the displaying: one creator reports not knowing how to get testimonials and not wanting to seem pushy, and another reports that praise never becomes a testimonial unless you ask, in the right way, at the right time. The ledger carries an exact, checkable mechanic for the ask that gets skipped — at most three follow-up emails, 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite, to customers who have not responded, plus a per-person pause. That reframes the second ask from a character problem into a setting, which is the most useful thing we can say to this reader with evidence she can check. Signup is the documented self-serve action and the fixed destination; the setting lives behind it.

emails.single_idea: The ask that produces the testimonial is usually the second one — and the second ask is a setting, not a question of nerve: up to three emails, 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite, and only to the students who have not answered.
emails.felt_need: "I know testimonials would help sell the next cohort. I don't really know how to get them, and I don't want to seem pushy asking my own students for reviews." [P1] And: the ones who loved it say so in passing and never send anything, because nobody asked again. [P3]
emails.status_quo: Asking by hand, once: a personal message when a student finishes, or a feedback box at the end of a chapter, and whatever comes back, comes back. (Audience-level, from creators who report collecting student feedback for their course and cohort pages — not a claim about this reader's own setup.)
emails.why_it_fails: When the ask is manual, the second ask is a fresh decision every time: you have to remember who answered, decide whether chasing this particular student is acceptable, and then do it on a day you feel like it. That is work that reliably gets postponed, which is why the first ask is usually also the last one.
emails.mechanism: In Senja you invite students individually or in bulk, and you switch the follow-ups on as part of the invite rather than deciding later: up to three reminder emails, sent 1, 3 and 7 days after the original invite, going only to the students who have not responded. If there is one student you would rather not remind, you pause reminders for that person without turning follow-ups off for everyone else. The schedule is fixed, so the decision is made once, before anything sends — which means it needs a Senja account and a form in it first; that is what the free plan is for.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: The same reader's second verified problem is format and permission, not persistence: should she ask for video or writing, and where does it go. Senja's form settings answer that exactly — a question can be set to Video (the student must record or upload), or to Video and text (the student picks one format, not both), and the consent page is on by default so the student chooses public or private use. Paired with the documented student-side effort (text or video, about 30 seconds, no account and no special software), that is a different, independently useful reason to open an account: you decide the format and the permission question before you ask a single student.
alternative_arguments.single_idea: You do not have to guess whether to ask for video or writing — it is a per-question setting, and the student's permission is a page that is already on by default.
alternative_arguments.felt_need: "Do I ask for video testimonials or just written ones? And am I allowed to put what they send me on my sales page?" [P2]
alternative_arguments.status_quo: An open-ended request — tell me what you thought — which leaves both the format and the permission to the student's judgment.
alternative_arguments.why_it_fails: An open request makes the student choose the format in the moment, and most people default to the easiest thing they can type; it also leaves you asking for permission to publish afterwards, as a second conversation.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: Each question in a Senja form has a format setting: Video means the student records or uploads a video, Video and text means they pick one of the two for that question — never both on the same question, so if you want a clip and a written line you ask them as two questions. Every question you show is required, and the student's name always is, so you decide the length of the ask by deciding how many questions to show. On the student's side it is a personalised page: text or video, about 30 seconds, no account and no special software. The consent page is enabled by default and lets them choose public or private use, so permission is part of the submission instead of a follow-up email.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: deciding between video and written testimonials is a judgment call I keep deferring, and publishing what students send feels like a grey area. After: the format is a setting on each question, one question cannot take both formats, and consent is a default page the student answers while they submit.
must_not_say: Do not claim video converts better than text, or that either format is more persuasive to prospective students — not established.
Do not promise students will complete the form in 30 seconds; Senja describes the form that way, which is a description of the form, not a measured student result.
Do not imply a student can leave both a video and a written answer on the same question.
Do not present the default consent page as legal advice or as compliance with any particular regime.
Do not suggest questions can be made optional — they cannot.
alternative_arguments.objection: If every question I show is required, won't a longer ask just make students abandon it?
alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Whether to ask her students for video, for text, or to let them pick — and how many questions the ask should contain before she sends it.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: A free account lets her build the form and see the per-question format settings (Video, or Video and text), the required-answer behaviour, and the consent page that is on by default, plus the student-facing page as the student will receive it: text or video, no account, no software.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: It does not tell her which format her students will actually choose, how many will finish the form, or whether a video outperforms a written quote on her cohort page.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Put the reader's own open question in the subject — video or written — and signal that it is a setting rather than a debate. No urgency, no claim about which wins.

edits.line: Collecting text and video is on every plan, Free included — so you can build the video form and read the whole reminder schedule before a single email reaches a student.
edits.problem: This is the CTA's whole payoff and it promises only that she can read a schedule. All three cold readers stopped on the same gap — they cannot tell what the student actually receives or is asked, and "read the whole reminder schedule" answers a question nobody has. The licensed material already covers this: a form invite can be sent as a test to the project owner's own address (E34), the consent page is on by default and lets the student choose public or private use (R8), and a Video question means the student records or uploads from the link (R6).
edits.fix: Make the free account's payoff the inspection she actually wants: that she can see the invite and the follow-ups as her students will receive them, in her own inbox, before one goes out, and that the student's side is a link, a recorded or uploaded answer, and a consent choice. State only what those facts support — no claim about how students will react, how many answer, or what they will say.

edits.line: If a student says something you'd want on the page for your next cohort, getting it on camera is a second job.
edits.problem: The problem named here is the labour of capturing video, which paragraph two then solves (no account, no software, 30 seconds) — and that framing is what pushed every reader to "will my students record at all", a question this email is not licensed to answer. The problem the email is built to solve, and the one its own paragraph three turns on, is that the second ask is the one that never gets sent.
edits.fix: Open on the thing that does not get sent — asking the same student again — stated conditionally, without asserting an imminent launch, a past failed ask or a manual chase she performs today, so that the "it's a setting, not a decision you make student by student" turn follows from the line above it.

edits.line: The second ask is part of that invite rather than something you decide student by student afterwards: switch on up to three follow-up emails, sent 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite, and only to students who haven't answered.
edits.problem: Three consecutive paragraphs of reminder administration, and the sentence that carries the idea is built backwards — the mechanic arrives after a clause contrasting it with something she has not been shown doing. Two readers had to re-read it; two stopped at the sentence immediately after. The bounds (three at most, fixed days, only non-responders, pausable for one named student) are the answer to the control objection, but as laid out they read as setup chores rather than as limits that keep her in control.
edits.fix: Lead with the plain mechanic in one short sentence, then present the not-retroactive caveat and the single-student pause inside the same paragraph as the bounds of what goes out under her name — one paragraph of reminder detail, not three.

edits.line: P.S. On Free: one form, up to 15 text or video testimonials, no credit card, video downloads in SD. Starter is $29 a month.

events.body:
The first testimonial request is a short email. The second one — to the student who hasn't replied — is a decision you'd otherwise take again, student by student.

Senja is a testimonial tool: you email your students a form, and their answers come back as text or video. Set a question to Video and the student records or uploads one from the link.

The second ask is a setting on the invite: **up to three follow-ups, 1, 3 and 7 days after it**, only to students who haven't answered. Turn them on first — earlier invites don't get them — and pause one student's reminders without ending everyone's.

Before anything reaches a student, send yourself a test; that email goes to the project owner's address. From their side it is a link, a recorded or uploaded answer, and a consent page, on by default, where they choose public or private use.

A free account is enough to build the form, read the test invite in your own inbox and switch the follow-ups on before the first one sends.

The context and problem reports below describe observed members of this market, not established experiences or installed tools of this recipient. The campaign request controls which job this email addresses; do not require a link to an unrequested integration in your doubts or click requirements.
Observed context (inferred; applicability must be checked): The corpus supports course creators who collect student feedback for course marketing, including a newly launched creator unsure how to ask and established creators using testimonials on landing pages and course or cohort offers. It does not establish the narrower situation of needing student videos before an imminent cohort launch.
Source: https://www.bmf.io/threads/what-are-the-best-ways-to-collect-testimonials-for-my-online-course.9780/; quote: I just launched my online course, and I know testimonials can help attract more students. The problem is, I don't know how to get them.
Source: https://codewithandrea.com/meta/my-2022-in-review/; quote: With this approach, I collected many great testimonials that I later placed on the course landing page.
Source: https://www.authorcirclehub.com/p/why-testimonials-are-the-most-underrated; quote: I have been collecting testimonials and using them on my Substack publication, my website, and across my offers, such as my course and cohort for the past six months.
Problem context: A newly launched course creator reports not knowing how to obtain testimonials and feeling reluctant to ask for reviews because it could seem pushy. [Source limits: Single-source problem; independent corroboration is not established.]; source: https://www.bmf.io/threads/what-are-the-best-ways-to-collect-testimonials-for-my-online-course.9780/
Problem context: The same creator is unsure whether incentives would seem fake, whether to request video or written testimonials, and where to collect and display them. [Source limits: Single-source problem; independent corroboration is not established.]; source: https://www.bmf.io/threads/what-are-the-best-ways-to-collect-testimonials-for-my-online-course.9780/
Problem context: Neera reports that praise does not automatically become strong testimonials: asking appropriately and promptly matters, and delayed requests can produce weaker recollections. [Source limits: Single-source problem; independent corroboration is not established.]; source: https://www.authorcirclehub.com/p/why-testimonials-are-the-most-underrated
Qualified scope of the selected audience: cohort-based course operators. This narrows who you are; it does not establish installed tools, prior actions or desired reactions.
Reading emphasis: weigh the effort of the next step against its usefulness. Do not assume an installed tool, a switching project or an existing workflow beyond the profile.
readers.what_it_sells: A testimonial collection tool: I email my students a link/form, they answer in text or record a video, and the tool sends up to three automatic reminders to the ones who haven't replied — so I'm not chasing individual students by hand before launch.
readers.biggest_doubt: The P.S. says free covers 15 text or video testimonials but HD video exports need Starter at $29/month. If I'm collecting video specifically for a launch page, I can't tell from this whether the free video is usable — embeddable, downloadable, good enough to cut into a page — or whether I collect a cohort's worth and then discover I must pay to get them out in usable form. That gating, buried at the end, is the hesitation, not the price.
readers.stopped_at: Turn them on first — earlier invites don't get them — and pause one student's reminders without ending everyone's.
fixes: 'Turn them on first — earlier invites don't get them — and pause one student's reminders without ending everyone's.' — three ideas in one sentence; split into two, caveat first.
'Decide the second ask once, not per student' — the subject never says testimonials or video; put the thing I'm collecting into it.

'P.S. Free covers one form and 15 text or video testimonials; HD video exports come with Starter, $29 a month.' — move the video limit out of the P.S. and say plainly what a free-plan video can do (embed/share/download) versus what needs Starter.

'Before anything reaches a student, send yourself a test; that email goes to the project owner's address.' — 'the project owner's address' is internal vocabulary before I have a project; say 'your own inbox'.
